questions.question: What does the Arabic word 'al-Kawthar' literally mean, derived from the root 'k-th-r'?
options: The banner of praise on the Day of Judgment
questions.explanation: The Foundation layer explains that 'kawthar' is derived from the Arabic root 'k-th-r,' meaning abundance, increase, and overwhelming goodness. It encompasses both the river of Kawthar in Paradise and the broader spiritual abundance granted to the Prophet.

questions.question: True or false: According to the tafsir, the Qurayshi taunt that the Prophet was 'abtar' arose after the death of his son Qasim, with Al-As ibn Wa'il identified as the one who hurled the insult.
questions.explanation: The Foundation layer explains that when the Prophet's young son Qasim passed away, the Quraysh leaders, particularly Al-As ibn Wa'il, taunted the Prophet by calling him 'abtar,' meaning one cut off from legacy. Surah al-Kawthar was revealed in response.

questions.question: What role does the letter 'fa' (so/therefore) play at the beginning of 'fa-salli li-rabbika wa-anhar'?
options: It marks a new, unrelated topic
It establishes a cause-and-effect link: because of the abundance given, respond with worship
It signals an oath being sworn
It introduces a question to the Prophet
questions.explanation: The Foundation layer notes that the 'fa' is a consequential connector meaning 'therefore' or 'so,' establishing a cause-and-effect relationship: because the Prophet has received this overwhelming abundance, he should respond with complete devotion through prayer and sacrifice.

questions.question: True or false: Imam Muslim records a narration from Anas ibn Malik in which the Prophet himself described al-Kawthar as a river Allah promised him, with a cistern his community will come to on the Day of Resurrection.
questions.explanation: Imam Tabari in Jami al-Bayan cites the authoritative narration transmitted by Anas ibn Malik in the Sahih of Muslim, in which the Prophet described al-Kawthar as a river Allah promised him with abundant good, and as a cistern his community will come to on the Day of Resurrection.

questions.question: According to Imam Tabari and the majority of the Companions including Ibn Abbas and Mujahid, what does the command 'wa-anhar' primarily refer to?
options: Placing the hands on the chest during prayer
The slaughtering of sacrificial animals, especially during Eid al-Adha
Reciting Allah's name aloud in worship
questions.explanation: Imam Tabari records that the majority of the Companions and successors, including Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ata ibn Abi Rabah, and Qatadah, understood 'anhar' to mean the slaughtering of sacrificial animals (nahr al-budn), especially during the days of Eid al-Adha. Ibn Kathir confirms this view decisively, contrasting it with the Makkan polytheists who offered such acts to their idols.

questions.question: How does Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran characterize the response Allah commanded the Prophet to give to mockery and grief in this surah?
options: A call for armed resistance against the mockers
A public defense through eloquent argument
Turning entirely toward Allah through prayer and sacrifice rather than counter-hostility
Withdrawing from preaching until the persecution ended
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb argues that Allah instructed the Prophet not to retaliate or defend himself through argument, but to pray and sacrifice, turning entirely toward Allah. Qutb sees this as the highest form of strength: responding to human hostility with increased devotion to Allah rather than counter-hostility.

questions.question: True or false: Wahbah al-Zuhayli notes that the verse 'inna shani'aka huwa al-abtar' uses the emphatic 'inna' combined with the pronoun 'huwa' to make it specifically and exclusively the enemy of the Prophet who is the one cut off.
questions.explanation: Wahbah al-Zuhayli in Al-Tafsir al-Munir reflects on the rhetorical mastery of the closing verse, noting that the combination of 'inna' (indeed/verily) with 'huwa' (he himself) produces maximum emphasis: it is specifically, emphatically, and exclusively the enemy of the Prophet who is cut off, removing any ambiguity.
